title: Observability & Monitoring
blurb: Logs, metrics, and traces -- how you actually see what a running system is doing, decide what's worth alerting on, and debug fast when something breaks.

beginner: The three pillars: logs, metrics, traces

description: Logs, metrics, traces, SLOs and error budgets, alerting design, and incident response -- how real systems are watched, understood, and debugged in production.

lessons.title: Why observability, not just monitoring
objectives: Distinguish monitoring from observability as complementary framings, not opposing disciplines
Explain how monitoring vs observability changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect monitoring vs observability with known vs unknown failure modes and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Monitoring checks known signals against expected failure conditions -- 'alert me if CPU exceeds 90%,' a question you decided to ask in advance.
examples:
# monitoring: a question decided in advance
# 'alert if error rate > 1%' -- you already know what to watch for
#
# observability: a question you couldn't have predicted
# 'why did checkout get slow for exactly these users, starting exactly then?'
# -- answering this requires being able to explore, not just check a known signal
commonMistakes: Treating monitoring and observability as strictly separate, opposing disciplines -- in practice they're complementary framings of the same underlying data, not a choice between two camps.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to explain this distinction precisely (without overclaiming it as an absolute law) is a common, genuine interview question for backend and infrastructure roles.

lessons.title: The three pillars: logs, metrics, traces
objectives: Describe what each of the three traditional observability signal types captures, and their trade-offs
Explain how logs changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect logs with metrics and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Logs are discrete, timestamped records of specific events -- rich detail, but expensive to store and search at volume. Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time -- cheap to store and query, but you lose the individual event detail behind an aggregate number.
examples:
# same underlying problem (a slow request), three different signals:
# logs: 'request 8827 took 3.9s, database query returned an error at 14:32:07'
# metrics: 'p99 latency for /checkout jumped from 200ms to 4000ms starting at 14:32'
# traces: 'this ONE specific request spent 3.8s of its 3.9s total waiting on the database span'
commonMistakes: Assuming these three are the only possible observability signals that exist -- they're the traditional, practical model most tooling is built around, not an exhaustive, closed list.
lessons.careerRelevance: This vocabulary (logs/metrics/traces) is the shared baseline language of essentially every observability tool and team in the industry.

lessons.title: Metric types: counters, gauges, histograms
objectives: Distinguish what each metric type can and can't represent
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: Prometheus metrics.
Explain how counter changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect counter with gauge and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A counter only ever increases (except when reset, e.g. on a process restart) -- good for 'total requests served' or 'total errors,' where you care about a running total, not the current state.
examples:
# choosing the right type by what you actually need to know:
# 'how many requests have we served, ever?' -> counter (only grows)
# 'how many requests are in the queue right now?' -> gauge (goes up and down)
# 'what does our latency DISTRIBUTION look like?' -> histogram (buckets, not one number)
# a histogram lets you see 'most requests are fast, but 1% are very slow' -- an average alone hides this
commonMistakes: Using a single average latency number instead of a histogram/percentiles -- an average can look perfectly healthy while hiding a real subset of slow requests a histogram would reveal.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly choosing a metric type for a given signal is a common, practical decision in any real backend or infrastructure role. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Distributed tracing in depth
objectives: Explain span relationships and trace context propagation beyond the basic trace-ID intro
Explain how span changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect span with parent/child spans and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A trace represents one request's full journey; it's made up of spans, each representing one unit of work (a service call, a database query) with its own start time and duration. Spans have parent-child relationships -- a parent span's duration should contain its children's time windows, letting you see exactly where time was spent within a larger operation.
examples:
# a trace is a TREE of spans, not a flat list:
# root span: 'handle checkout request' (120ms total)
#   -> child span: 'call payment service' (80ms)
#   -> child span: 'call inventory service' (30ms)
# each child's time window must fit within its parent's -- that's what makes
# the waterfall view meaningful, not just a list of unrelated timings
commonMistakes: Forgetting to propagate trace context across an async boundary (a queue, a background job) -- the trace silently breaks into two disconnected pieces exactly at that boundary, hiding the full.
lessons.careerRelevance: This lesson goes deeper than the basic trace-ID introduction in the Distributed Systems course, which intentionally stops there and defers dashboards, alerting, and metrics to this dedicated course.

lessons.title: Correlation IDs across services
objectives: Distinguish a trace ID from a correlation ID used in logs
Explain how correlation ID changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect correlation ID with trace ID and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A trace ID is a specific concept from distributed tracing systems, tied to the span-based data model covered in the previous lesson. A correlation ID is a more general idea -- any identifier attached to a request and included in every log line it touches, letting you find all logs related to one request even without a full tracing system in place.
examples:
# correlation ID in logs (works without any tracing system):
# every log line for one request includes: correlation_id: 'req-8827'
# -- lets you grep/filter all logs for this ONE request, even with no tracing setup
#
# trace ID (specifically part of a distributed tracing system):
# tied to spans, parent/child relationships, and trace context propagation
# often the SAME value is reused for both purposes, but they're not always identical
commonMistakes: Assuming correlation ID and trace ID are always exactly the same thing -- many real systems use correlation IDs in logs without any distributed tracing system in place at all; the concepts.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correlation IDs are a lower-cost, simpler-to-implement first step many teams take before adopting full distributed tracing.

lessons.title: Dashboards: signal, not noise
objectives: Explain what makes a dashboard actually useful during an incident, versus decorative
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: Grafana dashboards.
Explain how signal vs noise changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect signal vs noise with incident-driven dashboard design and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A dashboard's job during an incident is to answer 'is something wrong, and roughly where' quickly -- not to display every metric that could theoretically be shown.
examples:
# the actual test for a dashboard:
# NOT: 'does this show every metric we collect'
# BUT: 'if this exact incident happened at 3am, could someone half-awake
# glance at this dashboard and know roughly where to look next'
# a 40-chart dashboard usually fails this test worse than a 5-chart one
commonMistakes: Adding every available metric to a dashboard 'just in case it's useful someday' -- this is exactly how dashboards become too noisy to actually help during a real, time-pressured incident.
lessons.careerRelevance: Dashboard design that genuinely helps during an incident (not just looks comprehensive) is a real, valued skill distinguishing mature observability practice. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: SLIs, SLOs & error budgets
objectives: Define SLI, SLO, and error budget precisely, and distinguish an SLO from an SLA
Explain how SLI changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SLI with SLO and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the actual measured signal -- e.g. the percentage of requests that succeeded.
examples:
# SLI: the measured signal itself -- 'currently 99.95% of requests succeed'
# SLO: the target -- 'we aim for 99.9% success, measured over a rolling 30 days'
# error budget: what the SLO permits -- 0.1% of requests over 30 days can fail
# before you've used your budget; SLA: a SEPARATE, often external/contractual promise --
# not automatically the same number or scope as your internal SLO
commonMistakes: Treating an SLO as identical to an SLA, or promising 100% reliability -- an SLO is an internal target with an explicit, stated measurement window; promising perfect reliability ignores that.
lessons.careerRelevance: SLOs and error budgets are the standard, shared vocabulary reliability-focused teams use to decide how much risk is acceptable when shipping changes.

lessons.title: On-call practices & escalation
objectives: Describe the observability-supported parts of incident response: ownership, escalation, handoff, runbooks
Explain how on-call ownership changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect on-call ownership with escalation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: On-call means someone owns responding to alerts during a defined period, with clear escalation if the first responder can't resolve it or needs help. A runbook -- a written guide for a specific alert, covering likely causes and first response steps -- turns a 3am page into a followable checklist instead of a cold start from scratch.
examples:
# a runbook turns a cold-start 3am page into a followable checklist:
# alert: 'checkout error rate > 5%'
# runbook: '1. check the database-latency dashboard\n2. check recent deploys\n3. if\nboth clear, escalate to database on-call'
# -- observability data (dashboards, traces) is what the runbook actually points to
commonMistakes: Writing an alert with no accompanying runbook -- the on-call engineer has to reconstruct the right response from scratch each time, instead of following what a previous incident already.
lessons.careerRelevance: Runbooks tied directly to specific alerts are standard, expected practice at any company running a real on-call rotation.

lessons.title: Telemetry aggregation & the cardinality problem
objectives: Distinguish log volume/indexing cost from metric label cardinality, and explain why both are cost problems but not the same mechanism
Explain how log volume vs metric cardinality changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect log volume vs metric cardinality with time-series explosion and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Log volume and metric cardinality are related cost problems, but they work through genuinely different technical mechanisms. Logs cost more as volume and the number of distinct indexed fields grow -- more raw data to store and search, and more indexed fields to maintain for fast querying.
examples:
# two DIFFERENT mechanisms, not the same problem in disguise:
# logs: cost grows with total log VOLUME and number of indexed fields
# metrics: cost grows because each unique LABEL-VALUE COMBINATION is a
# separate stored time series -- adding user_id (50,000 values) as a label
# multiplies your time-series count by 50,000, even if log volume didn't change at all
commonMistakes: Assuming logs and metrics share the exact same cost mechanism just because both get expensive at scale -- they're related problems (unbounded dimensionality) but technically distinct: logs.
lessons.careerRelevance: Misunderstanding this distinction is a common, genuinely costly real mistake -- teams have been surprised by bills after adding a seemingly harmless high-cardinality label to a metric.

lessons.title: Building an observability culture
objectives: Synthesize the course's ideas into a mindset: instrumentation is a first-class engineering responsibility, not an afterthought
Explain how observability as a first-class responsibility changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect observability as a first-class responsibility with instrumentation during development and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every idea in this course points to the same underlying practice: a system's observability isn't something bolted on after it breaks -- it's built in deliberately, as part of writing the code itself, the same way tests are.
examples:
# the reframe this whole course builds toward:
# NOT: 'add some logging after something breaks, so it doesn't happen silently next time'
# BUT: 'as I write this feature, what would I need to see to know it's working
# correctly in production, and to debug it fast if it isn't' -- asked BEFORE shipping,
# not after the first unexplained incident
commonMistakes: Treating observability as something to add only after an incident forces the issue -- by then, you're debugging blind exactly when you need the data most; strong teams instrument as they.
lessons.careerRelevance: This mindset -- treating visibility into your own system as a core engineering responsibility -- is exactly what distinguishes mature, production-ready engineering practice.

quiz.q: What's the practical difference between monitoring and observability?
options: They are strictly opposing disciplines
Monitoring checks known signals against expected conditions; observability supports investigating questions you didn't predict in advance
Observability replaces monitoring entirely
There is no meaningful difference

quiz.q: What does a counter metric guarantee?
options: It can go up or down freely
It only increases, except when reset
It always represents a percentage
It stores every raw event value

quiz.q: What does a histogram metric preserve that a counter or gauge doesn't?
options: The exact timestamp of every event
A distribution summarized into buckets, enabling percentile calculations
The user ID of every request
Nothing extra

quiz.q: Why must trace context be explicitly propagated across an async boundary like a queue?
options: It propagates automatically everywhere
Without explicit propagation, the trace breaks into disconnected fragments at that boundary
Async boundaries never affect tracing
Trace context is only needed within one service

quiz.q: Is a correlation ID always identical to a trace ID?
options: Yes, always
Not necessarily -- correlation IDs can exist in logs without a full distributed tracing system in place
Correlation IDs are only used in tracing systems
They are unrelated concepts

quiz.q: What makes a dashboard actually useful during an incident?
options: Showing every available metric
Answering 'is something wrong and roughly where' quickly, with a minimal set of well-chosen charts
Having as many charts as possible
Dashboards are not useful during incidents

quiz.q: What is an SLI?
options: A contractual promise to customers
The actual measured signal, e.g. the percentage of requests that succeeded
A synonym for SLA
An alerting threshold

quiz.q: What is an error budget?
options: A financial budget for cloud infrastructure
The amount of unreliability an SLO permits before the budget is used up
A synonym for SLA
A type of log field

quiz.q: Is an SLO the same thing as an SLA?
options: Yes, always identical
No -- an SLO is typically an internal target; an SLA is often an external, contractual promise
SLA is a subset of SLO
There is no difference in practice

quiz.q: Why can alerting purely on symptoms with no clear response path be harmful?
options: It's never harmful
It trains on-call engineers to ignore alerts, contributing to alert fatigue and missed real incidents
Symptom-based alerts are always more accurate
This only affects large companies

quiz.q: What's the trade-off between a low and high alert threshold?
options: No real trade-off exists
Low threshold catches incidents faster but creates more false positives; high threshold reduces noise but risks missing real incidents longer
High thresholds always catch more incidents
Low thresholds never cause false positives

quiz.q: What does a runbook provide during an incident?
options: A financial report
A written guide for a specific alert covering likely causes and first response steps
A synonym for a dashboard
Nothing useful

quiz.q: How does synthetic monitoring differ from a basic health check?
options: They are identical
Synthetic monitoring runs a realistic user-like action end to end, catching issues a simple health check would miss
Health checks are more thorough
Synthetic monitoring only checks CPU usage

quiz.q: Do logs create metric time series?
options: Yes, every log line becomes a time series
No -- log volume/indexing cost and metric cardinality are related but technically distinct cost mechanisms
Logs and metrics are the exact same system
Only structured logs create time series

quiz.q: What specifically causes metric time-series count to explode?
options: Total log volume
Adding a high-cardinality label (like user_id) multiplies the number of unique label-value combinations, each becoming a separate stored time series
The number of dashboards viewing the metric
The metric's retention period alone

quiz.q: What does increasing data retention trade off?
options: Nothing, retention is free
Storage cost against how far back you can investigate an issue
Retention only affects dashboard load time
Retention has no relationship to cost

quiz.q: What does sampling (e.g. recording 10% of traces) trade off?
options: Nothing meaningful
Reduced cost against the risk that a specific individual request you need later wasn't captured
Sampling only affects metrics, never traces
Sampling always improves accuracy

quiz.q: In a realistic multi-pillar incident diagnosis, what does a metric typically tell you first?
options: The exact root cause immediately
That something is wrong and roughly when, narrowing down where to look next
Nothing useful without traces
The exact database query that failed

quiz.q: Why might diagnosing an incident using only logs (without metrics or traces) be harder?
options: Logs are always sufficient alone
Each pillar answers a different part of the question; combining them is usually what leads to a fast, confident diagnosis
Logs are never useful for incidents
Metrics and traces are redundant with logs

quiz.q: What does 'observability as a first-class responsibility' mean?
options: Adding logging only after an incident forces the issue
Building in structured logging, metrics, and tracing as part of writing the feature itself, not as an afterthought
Observability is optional polish
Only dedicated SRE teams should think about observability

exercises.title: Distinguish monitoring from observability
exercises.prompt: A colleague says 'observability makes monitoring obsolete.' How would you correct this framing?
exercises.hint: they're complementary, not opposing -- monitoring checks known signals, observability supports investigating things you didn't predict; most real systems need both

exercises.title: Choose the right metric type
exercises.prompt: For (a) total requests served since startup, (b) current number of items in a queue, and (c) request latency distribution, which metric type fits each?

exercises.title: Diagnose a broken trace
exercises.prompt: A trace shows a request entering a message queue, but the trace disappears at that point and a new, unrelated-looking trace starts on the consumer side. What's the likely cause, and the fix?
exercises.hint: trace context wasn't propagated across the async/queue boundary; the fix is explicitly passing the trace context (e.g. in message headers) so the consumer continues the same trace

exercises.title: Distinguish correlation ID from trace ID
exercises.prompt: A simple system logs a correlation_id on every request but has no distributed tracing infrastructure at all. Is this system doing distributed tracing? Explain.
exercises.hint: no -- correlation IDs in logs are a simpler, separate concept from distributed tracing; they let you find related log lines without span/parent-child trace data

exercises.title: Fix a noisy dashboard
exercises.prompt: An on-call engineer says they can't find the relevant chart during incidents because the dashboard has 40 panels. What would you recommend?
exercises.hint: redesign around the specific questions an on-call engineer needs answered during an incident, cutting down to the minimal set of charts that actually answer them

exercises.title: Calculate an error budget
exercises.prompt: An API has a 99.9% SLO, measured over 100,000 requests in a 30-day window, with 150 failures observed. Compute the allowed bad events, consumed budget, and whether the budget is exceeded.
exercises.hint: allowed = 100,000 * 0.001 = 100 bad events; consumed = 150; budget is exceeded by 50 events (150% of budget consumed)

exercises.title: Distinguish SLO from SLA
exercises.prompt: A team says 'our SLO and SLA are always identical.' Is this necessarily true? Explain.
exercises.hint: not necessarily -- an SLO is typically an internal target a team sets for itself; an SLA is often an external, contractual promise to customers, and the two don't have to match exactly

exercises.title: Diagnose an alert-fatigue problem
exercises.prompt: An on-call rotation reports they've started ignoring most pages because so many turn out to be non-issues. What's the likely root cause, and how would you address it?
exercises.hint: likely alert fatigue from a threshold set too low or alerts with no clear response path; address by raising thresholds thoughtfully, requiring alerts to be actionable, and distinguishing page-worthy from dashboard-only signals

exercises.title: Choose an alert threshold trade-off
exercises.prompt: For a payment-processing system where missed incidents are very costly, would you lean toward a lower or higher alert threshold, accepting the corresponding trade-off? Justify.
exercises.hint: likely a lower threshold, accepting more false positives, since the cost of missing a real payment incident outweighs the cost of extra false alerts here -- a defensible, context-specific choice, not a universal rule

exercises.title: Write a runbook outline
exercises.prompt: Given an alert 'checkout error rate > 5%,' outline a short runbook: what would you tell an on-call engineer to check first, second, and when to escalate?
exercises.hint: e.g. 1) check recent deploys/config changes, 2) check the payment-service dashboard for anomalies, 3) if both are clear, escalate to the payment-service on-call

exercises.title: Distinguish health check from synthetic monitoring
exercises.prompt: A service's /health endpoint returns 200 OK, but users report checkout is broken. What's the gap, and what would have caught it?
exercises.hint: a basic health check only confirms the process is alive/responding, not that a full user-facing flow works; synthetic monitoring (simulating an actual checkout) would have caught this

exercises.title: Explain why logs don't create metric time series
exercises.prompt: A colleague assumes adding more structured log fields will also increase their metric time-series count. Correct this understanding.
exercises.hint: log volume/indexed-field cost and metric cardinality are related (both costly at scale) but technically distinct mechanisms -- logs don't create metric time series; that's driven specifically by unique label-value combinations on metrics

exercises.title: Calculate metric cardinality
exercises.prompt: A metric has labels: service (4 values), endpoint (12 values), status (5 values). What's the time-series count? What happens if you add user_id with 20,000 distinct values?
exercises.hint: 4*12*5 = 240 time series; adding user_id multiplies this to 240*20,000 = 4,800,000 -- a massive, often unintended cost increase

exercises.title: Choose retention vs sampling trade-offs
exercises.prompt: A team needs to reduce observability costs. Compare reducing trace retention from 90 to 14 days versus sampling traces at 10% -- what does each actually sacrifice?
exercises.hint: reduced retention sacrifices ability to investigate OLDER incidents; sampling sacrifices having full detail on EVERY individual request, meaning a specific request you need later might not have been captured

exercises.title: Walk through a multi-pillar diagnosis
exercises.prompt: Given: a latency metric spike at 14:32, a trace showing 3.8 of 3.9 seconds spent in a database span, and a database log showing 'connection pool exhausted' at 14:32 -- walk through how each pillar contributed to the diagnosis.
exercises.hint: metric: told you something was wrong and roughly when; trace: narrowed down WHERE in the request path (database span specifically); logs: gave the specific, detailed reason (connection pool exhaustion)

exercises.title: Diagnose using only one pillar
exercises.prompt: A team tries to diagnose a slow-checkout incident using only aggregate metrics, with no traces or logs. What are they likely to be missing?
exercises.hint: metrics alone tell you THAT something is wrong and roughly when, but not WHERE in the request path (needs traces) or the specific detailed cause (needs logs)

exercises.title: Apply the observability-culture mindset
exercises.prompt: A team only adds logging and metrics to a feature after its first production incident. How would you reframe their approach going forward?
exercises.hint: build in structured logging, meaningful metrics, and tracing AS the feature is built, asking 'how will we know if this breaks' before shipping, rather than adding it reactively after the first incident

exercises.title: Design an SLO with a stated measurement window
exercises.prompt: Define an SLO for a search API, including the specific metric, the target percentage, and an explicitly stated measurement window.
exercises.hint: e.g. '99.5% of search requests return within 500ms, measured over a rolling 30-day window' -- the specific metric, target, and window must all be stated explicitly, not left implicit

projects.desc: Convert free-text log lines in a simple service to structured, queryable key-value logs.

projects.title: Simulate a trace propagated across 3 services

projects.title: Design an alerting policy that avoids alert fatigue
projects.desc: Design an alerting policy for a noisy metric, explicitly justifying the chosen threshold's false-positive vs missed-incident trade-off.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between monitoring and observability, and why aren't they opposing disciplines?
interviewPreparation.a: Monitoring checks known signals against expected failure conditions -- a question decided in advance. Observability supports investigating questions that weren't predicted ahead of time. They're complementary: monitoring catches what you already know to watch for, and observability lets you investigate what you didn't anticipate. Most real production systems need both, not a choice between them.

interviewPreparation.q: Explain the difference between an SLI, an SLO, and an error budget, and how an SLO differs from an SLA.
interviewPreparation.a: An SLI is the actual measured signal (e.g. percentage of successful requests). An SLO is the target for that signal, always with a stated measurement window (e.g. 99.9% over 30 days). An error budget is the amount of unreliability the SLO permits before it's exceeded. An SLA is typically a separate, often external contractual promise to customers -- it isn't automatically identical to the internal SLO a team sets for itself.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does adding a high-cardinality label like user_id to a metric cause costs to explode, and why is this a different mechanism from log costs?
interviewPreparation.a: Every unique combination of label values on a metric becomes a separate stored time series. Adding a label with 50,000 distinct values multiplies the existing time-series count by 50,000, not just adding a bit more data. This is a genuinely different mechanism from log costs, which scale with total log volume and the number of indexed fields -- logs don't create metric time series; the two are related cost problems (unbounded dimensionality) but technically distinct.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you avoid alert fatigue without missing real incidents?
interviewPreparation.a: Make every alert actionable with a clear response path, rather than alerting on raw symptoms with no next step. Distinguish page-worthy alerts (something needs immediate human response) from dashboard-only signals (worth tracking but not worth waking someone up for). Tune the threshold deliberately, understanding the specific trade-off between catching incidents faster (more false positives) and reducing noise (risk of missing real incidents longer) -- there's no universal correct threshold, it depends on the system's tolerance for each kind of mistake.

interviewPreparation.q: Walk through how you'd diagnose a real production incident using logs, metrics, and traces together.
interviewPreparation.a: Typically start with a metric showing something's abnormal (a latency spike, an error rate jump) -- this tells you something is wrong and roughly when. Then use a trace from around that time to see exactly where in the request path time was spent or a failure occurred. Then use logs from that specific service and time window to find the precise, detailed reason. No single pillar usually tells the whole story alone -- combining them is what leads to a fast, confident diagnosis.

capstone.title: Instrument and Operate a Production-Ready Service
capstone.description: Take a service (existing or new) and make it genuinely observable: structured logging, at least one SLI/SLO pair with a correctly derived error budget over a stated measurement window, an alerting policy with an explicit sensitivity trade-off, a signal-selection explanation for what a dashboard should show, and a written incident-response walkthrough combining logs, metrics, and traces. No paid cloud services or external vendor accounts are required -- everything can be designed and simulated.
deliverables: Structured (key-value) logging design for the service's key events
At least one defined SLI and SLO, with an explicitly stated measurement window
A correctly derived error budget for that SLO, with the calculation shown
An alerting policy with a stated threshold and an explicit false-positive vs missed-incident trade-off justification
A dashboard or signal-selection explanation: which specific signals were chosen and why, not just 'show everything'
A written incident-response walkthrough using logs, metrics, and traces together to reach a root cause
One intentionally simplified or manual component (e.g. no distributed tracing yet, or manual on-call handoff), with a stated justification for keeping it simple
capstone.portfolioTips: The intentionally-simplified component is the detail that separates 'I know observability concepts' from 'I understand what to actually prioritize first' -- explaining why you deliberately deferred something (and what you'd add next) reads as far more credible than claiming a fully complete setup.
